value: How did operant conditioning of spinal reflexes develop from a basic-science model of learning and memory into a clinical rehabilitation therapy, and what does that trajectory show about the relationship between basic and clinical research?

A mini review tracing 35 years of spinal reflex operant conditioning from a basic-science model of CNS memory (monkey, rat, mouse, human versions) through mechanistic work on a brain-spinal cord hierarchy of plasticity to its emerging use as a targeted-neuroplasticity therapy after incomplete spinal cord injury.

quote: This review tracks the evolution of another basic science exploration of spinal cord plasticity into a promising new clinical therapy.
As it has turned out, operant conditioning of spinal cord reflexes is both a valuable laboratory model and a potentially powerful therapeutic method.
Here we review the 35-year evolution of one promising new approach, operant conditioning of spinal reflexes.

value: The reward contingency induces plasticity in the brain, which in turn guides and sustains the spinal cord plasticity that directly produces the reflex change — a top-down hierarchy rather than a single site of change
quote: Taken together, these studies showed that H-reflex conditioning depends on a hierarchy of plasticity (i.e., Figure 2C), in which the reward contingency produces plasticity in the brain that guides and maintains the plasticity in the spinal cord that is directly responsible for the H-reflex change

value: Acquiring a new spinal behaviour disturbs the equilibrium serving existing behaviours, which triggers widespread adaptive change until a new equilibrium serving the enlarged repertoire is reached — and that renegotiation can repair a behaviour that trauma had impaired
quote: When the acquisition of a new behavior (e.g., a larger or smaller H-reflex) changes the spinal cord and disturbs older behaviors, it triggers widespread adaptive changes that arrive at a new equilibrium that serves the expanded repertoire.

The essential attribute of these protocols is that they base reward on the activity in a specific CNS pathway (e.g., the soleus H-reflex pathway, a corticospinal pathway). Thus, they produce “targeted neuroplasticity.”
